subject: language_arts

unit.title: Apostrophes & homophones
unit.essentialQuestion: When does a word need an apostrophe, and how do I pick between sound-alike words?

title: Homophones: there / their / they're
objectives: By the end, I can choose there, their or they're by meaning.

vocabulary.definition: words that sound the same but are spelled differently and mean different things
a place — and here is hiding inside it
belonging to them — it has heir (an owner) inside
squashed they are — the apostrophe stands for the missing a

emphasize: All three sound identical — choose by MEANING, never by sound.
The memory hooks: there has here inside (place); their has heir inside (an owner — belonging); they're is squashed they are.
The best test: can I say 'they are'? Then it's they're. Pre-empt defaulting to there for all three.

keyConcepts: there = place, their = belonging, they're = they are
misconceptions: writing they're without the apostrophe, or using it where nothing is squashed
hooks: These are the words grown-ups muddle most — even in text messages. Become the expert who never gets them wrong!

digital: three cue cards on screen (place / belonging / they are)

video.searchTerm: homophones there their they're song KS1
video.watchTask: Each time one of the three words appears, call out which one it is — place, belonging, or 'they are' — before the singer explains it.

afterCheck.question: Which of the three has an apostrophe, and why?
afterCheck.expectedAnswer: they're — because it's squashed 'they are' and the apostrophe marks the missing a

plan.goal: Set the challenge — three identical-sounding words that even grown-ups muddle; retrieve they're as a squash from Lesson 11.
plan.note: The beat-the-grown-ups frame carries the lesson. Read all three aloud to prove they sound identical.
plan.successCriteria: Child answers they're for the retrieval and accepts the expert challenge.

script.say: Three words sound EXACTLY the same — there, their, they're — but they mean completely different things. They're the words grown-ups muddle most, even in text messages! Today you're going to become the expert who never gets them wrong. Ready to beat the grown-ups? Warm-up first: one of them is a squashed-up pair. They are squashes into…?
script.adaptHints: Listen for they're. If shaky, re-show they are → they're, apostrophe for the missing a. Read the three words aloud identically — 'hear that? Identical. But watch the spellings.'

stuckProtocol: If they're won't come: write they are, cross the a, place the apostrophe — 'we buried this letter in Lesson 11, remember the gravestone?'

plan.goal: Teach the three meanings with their hidden-word hooks and the 'say they are' test.
plan.note: Circle here inside there and heir inside their; show they + are for they're. Model on the end-of-unit sentence.
plan.successCriteria: Child can recite: there = place (here inside), their = belonging (heir inside), they're = they are.

script.say: Pick by MEANING. There — a PLACE, like 'over there'. See the secret? Here is hiding inside there — both are about place. Their — BELONGING to them, 'their dog'. It's got heir in it — an heir is someone who owns things — so their is about owning. They're — squashed they are — the apostrophe stands for the missing a. My best test: can I say 'they are'? If yes, use they're. If it's a place, there. If it belongs to them, their. Watch me on a whole sentence: They're going to their house over there.
script.adaptHints: Trace the hidden words with your voice: 't-HERE', 'the-HEIR'. Say the test as a chant the child can echo.

blocks.definition: words that sound the same but are spelled differently and mean different things

blocks.caption: Say 'they are' — if it fits, it's they're. Place = there. Belonging = their.

plan.goal: Shared choices with the test said aloud: '___ my best friends' and 'I like ___ new car'.
plan.note: The child runs the test out loud before choosing, every time.
plan.successCriteria: Child fills both gaps correctly, saying the test aloud.

script.say: Choose with me. '___ my best friends.' Try the test — can I say 'they are my best friends'? Yes! So it's they're. Now this one's yours: 'I like ___ new car.' Does the car belong to them? Run the test out loud and pick.
script.adaptHints: If the child picks silently, gently require the spoken test: 'say the test first, then choose.' Swap 'car' for something the child's friends or family own.

check.question: Which of the three means 'belonging to them'?

wrongAnswers.remedy: Does 'over there' mean belonging? No — that's a place. Belonging is the one with heir inside.
Say 'they are' — does 'belonging to them' mean 'they are'? No. Which one has the owner hiding inside it?

plan.goal: Diagnostic: identify the belonging one and its hidden clue.
plan.note: The probe after a correct answer: 'what's the clue word hiding inside it?' (heir).
plan.successCriteria: Child picks their and names the heir clue.

script.say: Expert exam: which of the three means 'belonging to them'? And for a bonus point — what's the clue word hiding inside it?
script.adaptHints: Listen for their + heir. If the clue won't come, cover the t of their with a finger on screen and read what's left.

blocks.explain: their has heir inside — an heir is someone who owns things. Belonging = their.

check.question: Which of the three means 'belonging to them'?
check.expectedAnswer: their (heir — an owner — is hiding inside)

wrongAnswers.remedy: Does 'over there' mean belonging? No — that's a place. Belonging is their, with heir inside.
Say 'they are' — does 'belonging to them' mean 'they are'? No. Their is the belonging one.

plan.goal: Independent gap-filling: six gaps across all three words, the test said aloud each time.
plan.note: Director draws from practiceBank, start level 2. Watch for defaulting to there and for they're losing its apostrophe.
plan.successCriteria: Child chooses correctly in 4+ of 6 gaps, applying the spoken test.

script.say: Expert duty! Six sentences, each with a gap. For every one, say the test aloud — can I say 'they are'? is it a place? does it belong to them? — then choose. Beat the grown-up texters!
script.adaptHints: Theme sentences around the child's friends, pets and favourite places. Never change the target homophones.

stuckProtocol: Step down: give two choices instead of three; show the cue cards.
ONE hint: 'try saying they are in the gap — does it make sense?'
Keep it safe: 'Even grown-ups muddle these — the test makes you the expert.'

plan.goal: Child teaches back the three meanings and the test; end on a win.
plan.successCriteria: Child states: there = place (here inside), their = belonging (heir inside), they're = they are; test = 'can I say they are?'

script.say: Teach me the three meanings and the best test. … Perfect: there is a place with here inside, their is belonging with heir inside, they're is squashed they are — and the test is 'can I say they are?'. You ran the test on every gap and chose by meaning — you're now the expert who beats the grown-up texters.
script.adaptHints: Tease Lesson 15: 'next time, three MORE sound-alikes — two, too and to — plus your favourite trick yet: the extra o for extra.'

wrongAnswers.remedy: Does the spot belong to them? No — it's a PLACE. Which word has here hiding inside it?
Try the test: 'put the box over they are'? Nonsense! It's a place — which one is the place word?

hints: Is the gap a place, a belonging, or 'they are'?
Place = the one with here inside.

reteach.say: 'Over there' is pointing at a PLACE — and place words stick together: here, there. See here hiding inside there? Whenever the gap is a spot you could point at, it's there.

block.caption: over t-HERE — a place you can point at

wrongAnswers.remedy: Run the test: 'they are going to the park' — does it fit? Yes! So which spelling means they are?

wrongAnswers.why: belonging chosen where nothing is owned
wrongAnswers.remedy: Does anything belong to them here? No — try saying 'they are' in the gap instead.

hints: Say 'they are' in the gap — does it make sense?
It fits — so you need the squashed one with the apostrophe.

reteach.say: The test does all the work: '___ going to the park' → 'THEY ARE going to the park' — perfect sense! So it's they're, the squash, with its apostrophe for the missing a.

rows: they are going to the park

wrongAnswers.remedy: Whose ball is it? It belongs to the children — which word has the owner (heir) hiding inside?
Test it: 'the children lost they are ball'? Nonsense! The ball BELONGS to them — pick the belonging one.

hints: Does the ball belong to them?
Belonging = the one with heir inside.

reteach.say: The ball belongs to the children — belonging! And the belonging word is their, with heir (an owner) hiding inside. Place? No. They are? No. Belonging? Yes — their.

block.caption: their ball — it belongs to them

wrongAnswers.remedy: Is the gap a place you could point at? No — the dog belongs to somebody. Which is the belonging word?
Say it: 'is they are dog friendly'? That can't be right. Run the belonging question instead.

hints: An owner is involved — find the word with heir inside.

reteach.say: Ask the three questions in order: Can I say 'they are'? — 'is they are dog friendly' — no. Is it a place? No. Does the dog belong to them? YES — so it's their. Three questions, one winner.

block.prompt: '___ late for school.' Can I say 'they are' in this gap?
block.explain: 'They are late for school' makes perfect sense — so the gap takes they're, the squashed they are.

wrongAnswers.why: didn't actually run the test out loud
wrongAnswers.remedy: Say the whole sentence with 'they are' in it: 'they are late for school.' Does that make sense? It does!

wrongAnswers.why: hunting for belonging where nothing is owned
wrongAnswers.remedy: What would belong to them here? Nothing! Try the test sentence out loud first.

hints: Say the full sentence with 'they are' in the gap.
If it makes sense, the squash wins.

reteach.say: The test is a real sentence you say out loud, not a guess: '___ late for school' → 'THEY ARE late for school.' It works! Whenever 'they are' fits, write they're — the apostrophe version.

block.caption: say the test sentence OUT LOUD, then choose

wrongAnswers.remedy: Does the rainbow belong to them? No — you're POINTING at a spot. Which word has here inside?
'Look over they are — a rainbow'? Nonsense! It's a place — the pointing word.

hints: Could you point your finger at it?
Pointing at a spot = there (with here inside).

reteach.say: 'Look over there' — you're pointing! Place words are a little family: HERE, tHERE, wHERE — they all share here. Pointing at a spot? there, every time.

practiceBank.skill: distinguish all three in one sentence

block.prompt: They're taking their dog over there. Which of the three words means the PLACE?
block.explain: over there = the place. they're = they are (taking), their = the dog belongs to them.

wrongAnswers.why: meanings not yet separated when all three appear together
wrongAnswers.remedy: Whose dog? THEIR dog — that one's belonging. Now which one could you point at?

wrongAnswers.why: confusing the squash with the place
wrongAnswers.remedy: Stretch they're back out: 'THEY ARE taking' — that's the squash. The place is the one at the end you could point to.

hints: Label each of the three as you read: squash? belonging? place?
The place is the spot you could point your finger at.

reteach.say: All three in one sentence — the expert's moment! Read it in slow motion: They're (they are — squash) taking their (belongs to them) dog over there (point at it — place). Every job filled, no muddle.

block.prompt: Write one sentence using all three: there, their AND they're.
block.sample: They're taking their dog over there.

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: A sentence using they're (=they are), their (belonging) and there (place) each correctly

wrongAnswers.answer: a sentence with the three swapped (e.g. Their going… over they're)
wrongAnswers.why: spelling by sound instead of meaning under writing load
wrongAnswers.remedy: Read your sentence back and test each one: stretch the squash, find the owner, point at the place. Fix any word doing the wrong job.
they're is squashed 'they are' — where did the a go? Mark its gap with the apostrophe.

hints: Start with 'They're…' — you know it means they are.
Then give them something that belongs to them, and a place to go.

reteach.say: Build it in three little steps: who's doing something? They're (they are)… what do they take? their dog (belongs to them)… where? over there (point!). Say it out loud, then write it — one job per word.

block.caption: squash + belonging + place = one expert sentence

practiceBank.skill: distinguish all three in one sentence

options: They're going to their house over there.
There going to they're house over their.
Their going to there house over they're.
They're going to there house over their.
block.explain: they are going → they're; the house belongs to them → their; the place → there.

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: They're going to their house over there.

wrongAnswers.answer: There going to they're house over their.
wrongAnswers.why: all three swapped — chosen by sound
wrongAnswers.remedy: Test the first word: can you say 'THEY ARE going'? Yes — so the sentence must START with the squash.

wrongAnswers.answer: They're going to there house over their.
wrongAnswers.why: the squash is right but place/belonging are swapped
wrongAnswers.remedy: Whose house is it? It belongs to them — that needs the heir word. And the spot at the end is the one you point at.

hints: Check word by word: squash, belonging, place.
'They are going' fits the start — which spelling is that?

reteach.say: This is the exact sentence from your unit challenge! Slow motion: 'THEY ARE going' → they're. 'to THEIR house' — belongs to them, heir inside. 'over THERE' — point at it, here inside. Squash, belonging, place — in that order.

adaptivity.levelUp: 2 consecutive correct at the current level → next level; at level 3, mix single gaps with all-three-in-one-sentence items.
adaptivity.levelDown: 2 misses on the same skill → run the item's reteach with the three-question routine spoken aloud (say 'they are'? a place? belongs to them?), then a level-1 item with two choices instead of three.
adaptivity.masterySignal: 4+ correct across levels 2–3 including at least one of each word and one all-three item → mastery ≥ 0.8 for 'there/their/they're'.
struggleProtocol: Step down: two choices instead of three; cue cards visible.
ONE hint: 'try saying they are in the gap — does it make sense?'
Keep it safe: 'Even grown-ups muddle these — the test makes you the expert.'
adaptivity.personalization: Fill gaps with the learner's friends, pets and favourite places ('They're taking their scooter over there'). The spoken test stays in every framing.
adaptivity.endOnSuccess: Finish on a winnable gap; praise the process — 'you ran the test on every gap and chose by meaning.'

differentiation.support: Two choices instead of three; meaning cue cards stay on screen; the tutor says the test, the child decides.
differentiation.stretch: Write one sentence using all three correctly ('They're taking their dog over there.') and explain each choice.

extension: Find one example of each word in a favourite book and explain why that spelling is right.
assessmentEvidence: Child chooses correctly in at least four of six gaps, applying the 'say they are' test, and can state the meaning of each word.
revisitLater: Lesson 15 brings to/too/two and reviews this set. End-of-Unit 3 check uses '___ going to ___ house over ___' (They're / their / there).
